title: Who Has Seen the Child Parted from His Mother
intro: Al-Mubarrad, who had the story from the poet's son Harun, says that Ibn al-Zayyat had a slave girl whom he cherished, the mother of his son Umar, and that she died while the boy was small. Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, quoting two other lines the poet wrote for her, gives her name as Sakrana, and Ibn Khallikan, who quotes part of this poem from the anthology al-Bari', says she left him a son of eight. The poem opens with the child waking in tears because every other mother spends the night beside her son. The poet then excuses his own weeping to two companions and asks them to wait while he turns aside to her grave, comes back to the boy who is too young to bear the loss, counts what he has lost in her, calls on his eyes to weep, and ends at the grave he has not visited. Al-Mubarrad called it poetry that comes close to the heart and compels belief, and the critic Ibn Rashiq counted it among the finest and most moving elegies for women.

translation: Has anyone seen the child parted from his mother,
his eyes streaming a little after he falls asleep?
1.sharh: He asks the listener to look at his small son, who has lost his mother: the boy barely falls asleep before he wakes in tears. The elegy begins with the child's grief before it speaks of the father's.

translation: He sees every mother, though not his own, and her son
spend the night beneath the dark, whispering together.
2.sharh: The child sees other mothers spend the night with their sons, talking softly together in the dark. Only his own mother is missing, and the closeness he sees in other homes makes his loneliness worse.

translation: He wails, in a voice whose sobbing has broken my heart,
and in a downpour of tears that flow and flow.
3.sharh: The father describes his son crying: a raised, grieving voice caught by sobs, and tears that will not stop. It is his own heart, he says, that the boy's sobbing has broken.

translation: He spent the night alone in bed, driven on
by the cares of a heart that never stops pounding.
4.sharh: The boy spends the night alone in his bed with no mother to hold him. Anxiety keeps stirring him so that he cannot rest, and his heart races all night with fear and loneliness.

translation: One bucketful of tears, if I pour it out,
or two buckets, and I would be healed.
5.sharh: Turning from the child to himself, he speaks of tears as water drawn and poured out by the bucket: a bucket or two of weeping would cure him. Weeping is his medicine, as he explains in the next line.

translation: So do not blame me, you two, for weeping: with these tears
I am only treating what you see in me.
6.sharh: He asks his two companions not to blame his tears: weeping is how he treats the grief they can see in him. The anthologist Ibn Dawud called the line an apology wrung out by the depth of grief.

translation: A place in the earth, its grave-niche dug
for one who held every place in my heart,
7.sharh: He speaks of her grave: a narrow niche cut into the earth for someone who filled every corner of his heart. The word “place” comes near the start of the line and again at its end, and the sentence runs on into the next.

translation: is the place that most deserves a visit and love.
Will you two wait for me if I turn aside there?
8.sharh: The grave deserves a visit and love more than any place on earth, and he asks his companions to wait if he leaves the road to stop there. His editor al-Jaburi contrasts Jarir, whom shame kept from his wife's grave.

translation: Suppose I resolve to bear her loss, since I am
hardy: who will give patience to a boy of eight?
9.sharh: A grown man may be strong enough to bear the loss, but a child of eight is not, and no one can lend him patience. Ibn Rashiq counted this line and the four after it among the most moving poetry of mourning.

translation: Weak as he is, he does not seek God's reward in patience,
nor take comfort from others in times of loss.
10.sharh: A bereaved adult can bear a death by hoping for God's reward for patience, or by remembering that others have suffered the same. The child can do neither; he has none of the comforts that grown people lean on.

translation: Who is there now for me to fill with hopes, and to keep
in store against the stumbles of the days and the turns of time?
11.sharh: He has no one left to fill with hopes or to count on when time trips him up: she was that one. No early commentator explains the line; al-Jaburi, his modern editor, reads it and the three after it as memories of his life with her.

translation: Who, when I came home, would honour the place I sat,
and when I was away, would watch over me and spare me every care?
12.sharh: He lists what he has lost in her: she honoured him at home and watched over his affairs when he was away. Al-Mubarrad follows the poem with another man's elegy for a wife who guarded him in his absence and gladdened him in his presence.

translation: I have never seen the like of fate, the way it strikes me,
nor of this age, the way it has shot at me,
13.sharh: He has never known anything as cruel as the fate that keeps hitting him, or as the times that have taken aim at him. Time is an archer, and he is its target.

translation: nor the like of the days whose loss has wounded me,
nor of the day that came after them and struck me down.
14.sharh: Nothing compares with the happy days he has lost, or the day after them that brought disaster. No early commentator explains it; most likely the days are his time with her, and the day the one on which she died.

translation: My eyes, if you will not help my tears today,
then whatever you promise me for tomorrow is worthless.
15.sharh: He calls on his eyes to help him weep today, since tears put off until tomorrow are a promise worth nothing. Grief is owed on the day of the loss, not after it.

translation: My eyes, if I announce the death of joy and its people
and of the days of my youth, they have announced mine already.
16.sharh: If he announces that joy and youth have died, they have already announced his death, for losing them is his own death. No early commentator explains it; the two who announce his death are most likely joy and youth.

translation: My eyes, if I weep for gladness and youth,
they have already given notice of leaving me, and wept for me.
17.sharh: If he weeps for gladness and youth, they have already told him they are leaving, and wept over him before he could weep over them: the same reversal as in the line before. The verb is the one used of a beloved who announces her departure.

translation: A house I have not visited: how much of my heart
has bound itself to it, and how it weighs on me.
18.sharh: The house is her grave. He has not visited it, yet his heart is bound up with it. Just before the poem, al-Mubarrad quotes two lines in which he answers friends who urge him to visit her grave: she has no grave but his heart.

translation: A house I have not visited: how precious is what
the two shrouds hold within it, beneath the earth.
19.sharh: The grave he has not visited holds what is most precious to him: her body in its two shrouds. The line repeats the opening of the one before, and the poem ends at the grave it first reached in line 7.

2.2.4.head: اِنتَجى
2.2.4.meaning: Whisper together, confide in each other.

3.2.1.head: سَحّ
3.2.1.meaning: A downpour. The reciter says it with -i, joining it to “in a voice”; both prints of al-Mubarrad have -u, making it a second subject: “his sobbing and the downpour of tears have broken my heart”.

4.2.1.head: بَلابِل
4.2.1.meaning: Cares, anxious thoughts that churn in the breast.

5.1.3.head: سِجل
5.1.3.meaning: Sijl, as the reciter says it, here and in the second half; the editions and the dictionaries have sajl, a large bucket full of water.

6.1.2.head: لَحا
6.1.2.meaning: Blame me, reproach me (said to two people).

7.1.5-6.meaning: “Its lahd was dug”: the lahd is the niche cut into the side of a grave, where the body is laid.

8.2.4.head: عاجَ
8.2.4.meaning: Turned aside to a place and stopped there.

10.1.6.head: حِسبَة
10.1.6.meaning: Hisba: bearing a loss patiently in hope of God's reward.

10.2.2.head: اِئتَسى
10.2.2.meaning: Takes comfort from the example of others who suffered the same.

11.2.3.head: صَرف
11.2.3.meaning: The turns of fortune, so called because they turn things from their course.

12.2.4.head: حاطَ
12.2.4.meaning: Guarded me, looked after my affairs.

14.2.6.head: دَهى
14.2.6.meaning: Struck me with a disaster, one that comes from where one felt safe.

15.1.3.head: أَسعَدَ
15.1.3.meaning: Help (said to two). The verb is used above all of helping a mourner weep, as women helped their neighbours keen.

17.2.2.head: آذَنَ
17.2.2.meaning: Gave notice; most likely of their leaving, as in the line “Asma' has given us notice of her parting”.

18.1.3.head: بَيت
18.1.3.meaning: A house: here, the grave. Jamil Sa'id's and al-Jaburi's editions of his poems have maytan, “a dead one”, here and in the next line.

19.2.5.head: الكَفَن
19.2.5.meaning: The two shrouds; kafan is the cloth a body is wrapped in for burial.
